notes:
Task and constraints: Return an (n-2) by (n-2) matrix where each cell is the maximum value in the corresponding 3-by-3 window of the input grid.
Idea: For each valid 3-by-3 window, inspect its nine cells and store their maximum at the corresponding output coordinate.
Technique and why it applies: Inspecting all nine cells of each window computes every required local maximum.
Invariant: Each output cell equals the maximum of the input cells in the window centered at that position.
Edge cases: The output dimensions are `(n-2) × (n-2)`; every window remains inside the grid.
Complexity: O(n²) time for fixed 3-by-3 windows and O(n²) output space.
complexity_reason: Inspecting all nine cells of each window computes every required local maximum.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum number of white blocks that must be recolored so some substring of length k contains only black blocks.
Idea: Count black blocks in the first window of length k, then slide one position at a time updating the count and minimizing `k-black`.
Technique and why it applies: Sliding-window updates evaluate every length-k window in constant time after initialization.
Invariant: The running count equals the number of black blocks in the current window, so its white count is k minus that value.
Edge cases: The first window is included; k may equal the string length; no window requires more than k recolors.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Sliding-window updates evaluate every length-k window in constant time after initialization.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum training hours needed so initial energy and experience exceed each opponent's corresponding values when encountered.
Idea: Train energy until it exceeds total opponent energy, then walk opponents in order and add enough experience to be strictly greater before each fight.
Technique and why it applies: Separate total-energy and sequential-experience calculations satisfy both strict victory conditions minimally.
Invariant: The energy requirement is based on total consumption; experience is updated after each opponent and training is added only when needed.
Edge cases: Both energy and experience must be strictly greater; after winning, add the defeated opponent's experience.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Separate total-energy and sequential-experience calculations satisfy both strict victory conditions minimally.

notes:
Task and constraints: Process the string where each '*' removes the closest preceding non-star character, and return the remaining string.
Idea: Scan characters into a stack or `StringBuilder`; on `*`, remove the last stored character.
Technique and why it applies: A stack makes the nearest preceding surviving character available for each star.
Invariant: The stack contains exactly the characters not yet removed from the processed prefix.
Edge cases: The input guarantees each star has a preceding removable character; multiple stars remove the nearest remaining characters in sequence.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: A stack makes the nearest preceding surviving character available for each star.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if two different length-two subarrays have the same sum.
Idea: Compute each adjacent pair sum and insert it into a set; return true when a sum is already present.
Technique and why it applies: Remembering previous adjacent sums detects duplicate pair totals in one pass.
Invariant: The set contains sums of earlier length-two subarrays, so a repeated sum proves two different subarrays match.
Edge cases: At least two elements are needed for a pair; equal sums at different indices qualify.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Remembering previous adjacent sums detects duplicate pair totals in one pass.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the even number with the highest frequency, choosing the smallest number when frequencies tie; return -1 if there is no even number.
Idea: Count only even values, then choose the value with greatest frequency and smallest numeric value on ties.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency comparison plus the smaller-value tie rule selects the required even element.
Invariant: The frequency map contains exactly the even elements; the selected candidate follows frequency-first and value-second ordering.
Edge cases: Return -1 if there are no even values; negative even integers are valid.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(u) space for u distinct even values.
complexity_reason: Frequency comparison plus the smaller-value tie rule selects the required even element.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the smallest positive integer that is divisible by both n and 2.
Idea: Return n if it is even; otherwise return `2*n`.
Technique and why it applies: Parity determines whether n itself works or must be doubled to become even.
Invariant: An even n is already divisible by both n and two; for odd n, twice n is the smallest common multiple.
Edge cases: n is positive; odd inputs need doubling and even inputs need no change.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Parity determines whether n itself works or must be doubled to become even.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the names sorted from tallest to shortest.
Idea: Pair each name with its height or sort original indices by descending height, then emit names in that order.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting by height while carrying the matching name preserves each person's association.
Invariant: Each output position contains the name associated with the corresponding height in descending order.
Edge cases: Names and heights align by index; equal heights follow the sort comparator's tie behavior.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary/output space.
complexity_reason: Sorting by height while carrying the matching name preserves each person's association.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of positive integers that divide both a and b.
Idea: Test every integer from one through `min(a,b)` and count those dividing both inputs.
Technique and why it applies: Checking divisors only up to the smaller input covers every possible common factor.
Invariant: Every common positive factor is no greater than the smaller number, so this range includes all candidates.
Edge cases: Both inputs are positive; one is always a common factor.
Complexity: O(min(a,b)) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Checking divisors only up to the smaller input covers every possible common factor.

notes:
Task and constraints: Given employees' task end times in chronological order, return the employee ID with the longest single task; choose the smallest ID on a tie.
Idea: Use each log's end time minus the previous log's end time as duration; update the winner for a longer task or a tie with smaller employee ID.
Technique and why it applies: Consecutive end-time differences give task durations, and explicit tie-breaking selects the required employee.
Invariant: The best candidate tracks the longest duration seen, with smaller ID as the tie-breaker.
Edge cases: The first task starts at time zero; logs are chronological; ties must prefer the smaller employee ID.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Consecutive end-time differences give task durations, and explicit tie-breaking selects the required employee.
